units.translation: But about Prometheus, as we see in Apollodorus 1, 7, 1, three fables were treated by Aeschylus, in two tragedies, Prometheus Bound, which survives, and Prometheus Unbound, and in one satyr play, which was inscribed by Aeschylus with the simple name Prometheus, Prometheus the Fire-Bearer by the Alexandrian grammarians. About these fables the writer of the Life of Aeschylus in the Scholia, ed. Oxon. p. 8, 1 says: ταύτῃ καὶ ἄριστος εἰς τραγῳδίαν Αἰσχύλος κρίνεται, ὅτι εἰσάγει πρόσωπα μεγάλα καὶ ἀξιόχρεα. καὶ τινὲς ἤδη τῶν τραγῳδιῶν διὰ μόνων οἰκονομοῦνται τῶν θεῶν, καθάπερ οἱ Προμηθεῖς [In this way Aeschylus is judged best in tragedy, because he introduces great and worthy characters. And some of the tragedies are managed by the gods alone, as the Prometheus plays]. But about the vain opinion of many, who have imagined that a tetralogy Promethea was composed of three tragedies, Prometheus the Fire-Bearer, Bound, Unbound (although in the Bound the affairs of Prometheus are so set forth that no other fable appears to have preceded), and an unknown satyr play, but that the satyr drama Prometheus, which we know was performed in Olympiad 76, 4 with three tragedies (Phineus, Persians, Glaucus), was not Prometheus the Fire-Bearer, but Pollux (9, 156) Prometheus the Fire-Kindler, of whom no other witness is ever produced, they have believed; I have said in the Life of Sophocles, ed. Oxon. a. 1860, vol. 8 p. LXII, where I have revealed the origin of the error committed by Pollux. Others have believed that Prometheus the Fire-Bearer was the third play of the tetralogy, the name being imposed not on account of the theft of fire, but referring to the torch-races celebrated at Athens every year in honor of Prometheus: which institution could have been mentioned in the final part of Prometheus Unbound (in which also there was a speech about the crown for Prometheus: see fr. 204), as the honors to be given to the Eumenides are set forth at the end of the play of that name, which is closed with a solemn procession, but how it could have sufficed for the composition of a whole tragedy, and such as Aeschylus was accustomed to make, is not clear.
